title: Setup
body_md:
We evaluate four finite-state benchmarks (two-state control, cybersecurity, distribution planning, advertising) and three continuous-state benchmarks (linear--quadratic (LQ) control, portfolio, bimodal allocation). The results for cybersecurity and advertising are presented in Appendix~\ref{app:additional-results}. Baselines are REINFORCE, MF-REINFORCE \citep{meunier2026model} on finite states, and, on LQ control and portfolio, Transport-Proba, which replaces the centered differences by a likelihood-ratio estimate of the moment sensitivities, as per Appendix~\ref{eq : LQ-setting}. Methods share the policy class, initialization, number of updates and simulator budget. Results use five paired seeds.
We report $|J(\widehat\theta)-J(\theta^\star)|$, where $\widehat \theta$ is the final parameter returned by training and $\theta^\star$ maximizes the original, unperturbed objective $J$ over the benchmark's admissible policy class. Thus the reference $\theta^\star$ does not depend on $\lambda$, although the learned parameter does. Distribution planning uses a numerical reference.
Appendix~\ref{app:experiments} gives models, evaluation and settings. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/adonis107/RL-MFC-TransportREINFORCE}.

We write ${\cal P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for probability measures with finite second moment. 
Let ${\cal C}_c^1(D)$ denote the space of continuously differentiable functions with compact support over $D \subset \mathbb{R}^m$.
We use $|\cdot|$ for absolute values, $\|\cdot\|$ for Euclidean norms and operator norms of matrices, $\|\cdot\|_\mathrm{F}$ for the Frobenius norm, and $\|v\|_1 = \sum_i|v_i|$. Define

u)} \int_{\mathbb{R}^d	imes\mathbb{R}^d} \|x-y\|^2\gamma(\mathrm{d} x,\mathrm{d} y),

Finally, $\mathbb{S}^d$ denotes the set of symmetric  matrices over $\mathbb{R}^{d 	imes d}$ while $\mathbb{S}_{++}^d$ denotes the symmetric positive-definite ones. label: assumption:discrete-well-posedness
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{assumption:discrete-well-posedness}
The initial law $\mu_0\in\Delta_N$ is independent of $\theta$, and the policies and transition kernels are measurable. The rewards satisfy $|r_t(x_i,m,a)|\leq\overline r$ and $|g(x_i,m)|\leq\overline g$ uniformly in their arguments. For every $t,i,j \in \llbracket 0, T-1 \rrbracket \times \llbracket 1, N \rrbracket \times \llbracket 1, N \rrbracket$, the maps $(\theta,m)\mapsto K_t^\theta(x_j\mid x_i,m)$ and $(\theta,m)\mapsto R_t^\theta(x_i,m)$ are continuous on $\Theta\times\Delta_N$, and $m\mapsto g(x_i,m)$ is continuous on $\Delta_N$.
head: environment
name: Finite-state well-posedness

label: prop:discrete-well-posedness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:discrete-well-posedness}
Under Assumption~\ref{assumption:discrete-well-posedness}, the original process and its finite-state perturbation are uniquely defined in law. Their objectives $J$ and $J^\lambda$, $\lambda\in[0,1)$, are continuous on $\Theta$ and bounded in absolute value by $T\overline r+\overline g$. In particular, they attain their maxima when $\Theta$ is non-empty and compact.

name: Explicit perturbation density

title: Proof
body_md:
For the fixed $z=(p,m,\Sigma)$, consider the map $\Psi_\lambda(z,\cdot)$ from~\eqref{eq:continuous-perturbation-map}:
    \begin{align}
        \Psi_\lambda(z,(q,a,b))=\Big(
        (1-\lambda)p+\lambda q,\,
        (1-\lambda)m+\lambda a,
        \big(
            \Sigma_j^{1/2}
            ((1-\lambda)I_d+\lambda b_j)^2
            \Sigma_j^{1/2}
        \big)_{j=1}^K
    \Big).
    \end{align}
    For $b_k\in{\cal B}_\lambda$, the matrix $(1-\lambda)I_d+\lambda b_k$ is positive definite. The square map is a smooth diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{S}_{++}^d$ onto itself, with inverse given by the positive definite square root. Thus the displayed map is a smooth diffeomorphism from $\Delta_K^\circ\times(\mathbb{R}^d)^K\times({\cal B}_\lambda)^K$ onto ${\cal Y}_t^{\lambda,\theta}\times(\mathbb{R}^d)^K\times(\mathbb{S}_{++}^d)^K$, with the inverse given by~\eqref{eq:continuous-inverse-coordinates}.

    For each $j$, let $F_j$ be the covariance map $F$ of Lemma~\ref{lemma:covariance-jacobian} with $\Sigma=\Sigma_j$. Each output block depends only on its corresponding input block. Hence, in the free weight, mean, and independent covariance coordinates, the Jacobian matrix is block diagonal:
    \begin{align}
        D_{(q,a,b)}\Psi_\lambda(z,(q,a,b))
        =\operatorname{diag}\big(\lambda I_{K-1},\lambda I_{Kd},DF_1(b_1),\ldots,DF_K(b_K)\big).
    \end{align}
    Its determinant is therefore the product of the block determinants. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:covariance-jacobian},
    \begin{align}
        \det D_{(q,a,b)}\Psi_\lambda(z,(q,a,b))
        &=\lambda^{K-1}\lambda^{Kd}\prod_{j=1}^K\det DF_j(b_j)\\
        &=\lambda^{(K-1)+Kd+Kd(d+1)/2}\prod_{j=1}^K
        \bigg[(\det\Sigma_j)^{(d+1)/2}\prod_{i=1}^d(2c_{j,i})\prod_{1\leq i<\ell\leq d}(c_{j,i}+c_{j,\ell})\bigg]\\
        &=\mathcal J^\lambda(z,b)>0,
    \end{align}
    since $q_K=(K-1)+Kd+Kd(d+1)/2$. For $K=1$, the weight block is omitted. The change-of-variables formula, together with $f_{(Q,A,B)}=f_Qf_Af_B$, now gives~\eqref{eq:continuous-explicit-density}.

label: assumption:continuous-likelihood-ratio-regularity
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{assumption:continuous-likelihood-ratio-regularity}
\
\begin{enumerate}
    \item [(1)]  For every $t\in\llbracket 0,T-1\rrbracket$ and for every $(x,\mu,a) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times {\cal P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d) \times {\cal A}$, and every admissible $z \in \widetilde{{\cal Z}}_K$, the maps
$
\theta\longmapsto p_t^\theta(a\mid x,\mu)$ and 
$\theta\longmapsto h^\lambda(y\mid z_{K,t+1}^\theta)$ 
are of class ${\cal C}^1(\Theta^\circ)$, where $\Theta \subset \Theta^{\circ} $, is an open set and strictly positive. This requires the map $\theta \mapsto z_{K,t}^{\theta} \in \widetilde{{\cal Z}}_K$ to be ${\cal C}^1(\Theta^{\circ})$. Moreover, they satisfy sufficient regularity conditions to justify differentiation under the integral sign and the corresponding score-function identities, namely existence of an integrable function $G_\theta$ such that the relevant derivatives are uniformly dominated by $G_\theta$. 
   \item [(2)] Moreover, we assume that
    \begin{align}
       \underset{\theta \in \Theta}{\text{ sup }} \mathbb{E} \Big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \lVert \nabla_{\theta} \text{ log } p_t^{\theta}(X_t, {\cal D}_{K}(Q_t,M_t,\Sigma_t), A_t) \rVert^2 + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \lVert \nabla_{\theta} \text{ log } h^\lambda(Q_t, M_t,\Sigma_t \mid z_{K,t}^\theta) \rVert^2 \Big] < \infty
    \end{align}
    \item[(3)]
    Denote by $S$ the trajectory random variable
    \[S :=
        \big(
    X_0^{K,\lambda,\theta},
            \alpha_0^{K,\lambda,\theta},
            X_1^{K,\lambda,\theta},
            \ldots,
            \alpha_{T-1}^{K,\lambda,\theta},
            X_T^{K,\lambda,\theta},
            Z_{K,1}^{\lambda,\theta},
            \ldots,
            Z_{K,T}^{\lambda,\theta}
        \big),\]
    and define its law by $\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\theta}:={\cal L}(S)$.
    We assume that ${\cal R}(S) \in L^2(\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\theta})$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Likelihood-ratio representation

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\lambda\in(0,1)$. Write a trajectory as $s=(x_0,a_0,x_1,\ldots,a_{T-1},x_T,z_1,\ldots,z_T)$. For $t\in{\cal T}$, define the population-argument map $m_t : \widetilde {\cal Z}_K^T \to {\cal P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ by
\begin{align}
    m_0(z_1,\ldots,z_T) = \mu_0,\qquad
    m_t(z_1,\ldots,z_T) = {\cal D}_K(z_t),\quad
    t\in\llbracket1,T\rrbracket
\end{align}
We abbreviate these arguments as $m_t$. In particular, the initial population argument is kept exact and is not projected onto the Gaussian-mixture family.

Recalling the policy reference measure $\nu_A$ introduced in Section~\ref{sec:background}, define
\[
    \nu(\mathrm{d} s)
    :=
    \mu_0(\mathrm{d} x_0)
    \prod_{t=1}^T \mathrm{d} z_t
    \prod_{t=0}^{T-1}
    \left[
        \nu_A(\mathrm{d} a_t)
        P_t(\mathrm{d} x_{t+1}\mid x_t,m_t,a_t)
    \right].
\]
By independence of the randomizers, the trajectory law is
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\theta}(\mathrm{d} s)
    :={\cal L}(S)(\mathrm{d} s)
    =\ell^{\lambda,\theta}(s)\nu(\mathrm{d} s),
\end{align}
where $  \ell^{\lambda,\theta}(s)
    =
    \prod_{t=0}^{T-1}
        p_t^\theta(a_t\mid x_t,m_t)
    \prod_{t=1}^T h^\lambda(z_t\mid z_{K,t}^\theta)$.
Here the return uses the same population arguments,
\[
    {\cal R}(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r_t(x_t,m_t,a_t)+g(x_T,m_T),
\]
and is independent of $\theta$ when $s$ is held fixed. The reference measure $\nu$ is also independent of $\theta$. Hence, we have $ J_K^\lambda(\theta)
    =
    \int {\cal R}(s)\mathbb{P}^{\lambda,\theta}(\mathrm{d} s)
    =
    \int {\cal R}(s)\ell^{\lambda,\theta}(s)\nu(\mathrm{d} s)$. 
Now, under the Assumptions \ref{assumption: randomizer_rho}, \ref{assumption:continuous-likelihood-ratio-regularity}, we get with dominated convergence theorem that
\begin{align}
    \nabla_\theta J_K^\lambda(\theta)
    =
    \int
        {\cal R}(s)\nabla_\theta\ell^{\lambda,\theta}(s)
        \nu(\mathrm{d} s),
\end{align}
and we end using the \eqref{eq:continuous-main-score} term and $
    \nabla_\theta\log h^\lambda(z_t\mid z_{K,t}^\theta) =
    (D_t^\theta)^\top
    s^\lambda(z_t,z_{K,t}^\theta)$. The probabilistic representation follows by definition of the quantities.

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Theorem~\ref{theorem:continuous-pg-representation} with $K=1$. Each policy score has conditional mean zero given the history up to its action draw, and each population score has conditional mean zero given the history before its independent randomizer is drawn. Rewards at times $s<t$ are measurable with respect to these histories, so their products with the time-$t$ scores have zero expectation. Removing these past rewards gives the stated reward-to-go formula.

name: Simulation cost

title: Proof
body_md:
The population and online stages use $MT$ and $BT$ transitions, respectively. Fresh finite-state auxiliary batches require $n\sum_{t=1}^T t=nT(T+1)/2$ transitions, whereas a shared batch of $n$ trajectories of length $T$ requires $nT$ transitions.
    In continuous state space, the $2d_\theta$ auxiliary systems contain $n=2d_\theta n_0$ particles in total and require $nT$ transitions.
